title: Apollo 11 was heading for a boulder field until Armstrong took over and flew past it

cover.alt: View through the lunar module’s window, past its dark frame, of grey cratered ground and the shadowed rim of a crater below.

body: On 20 July 1969, the lunar module *Eagle* was coming down a little too fast: it passed landmarks two or three seconds early, which meant it would land miles beyond its target. Its guidance computer was also flashing **1202 and 1201 alarms**, because it had more tasks than it could finish in real time, but engineers on the ground judged it safe to carry on. Looking out, Neil Armstrong saw that the computer was steering for a boulder-strewn area near a 300-foot crater, later named West crater, so he took semi-automatic control and flew on to find clear ground. *Eagle* touched down at 20:17:40 UTC, with very little fuel to spare.

slides.alt: View from the lunar module’s window, with its dark frame on the left: grey cratered ground slides past below, the shadowed rim of a crater drifts by, then the ground comes closer, streaks of dust sweep across it and the lander’s shadow appears.
slides.caption: 20 July 1969, through Eagle’s window: craters slide past, then dust streams across the ground and Eagle’s shadow appears near touchdown. Filmed at 6 frames a second, it plays about 4× fast.
slides.credit: NASA · Public domain · excerpt, plays about 4× faster than real time

slides.question: The crew thought they had about 25 seconds of fuel left before an abort. What did later analysis find?
slides.explanation: Closer to 50 seconds. Still a thin margin: Eagle landed with 216 pounds (98 kg) of usable fuel.

slides.heading: Powered flight left before an unsafe abort
slides.note: The later figure is approximate: “closer to 50 seconds”

slides.question: What did Eagle’s 1202 and 1201 alarms mean?
options: The computer had too much to do
A leg had touched the ground
slides.explanation: They were “executive overflows”: the computer couldn’t finish all its tasks in real time. Engineer Jack Garman told guidance officer Steve Bales it was safe to continue.
